phase_label: Phase 3: Applied ML Scientist, AI Research Scientist, Research Engineer, NLP Engineer
intended_use: Detailed self-study reading materials aligned to the role/topic inventory used for the 12,000-question MCQ/MSQ bank.

schema.topics: Each topic module contains learning objectives, detailed reading notes, practice tasks, pitfalls, and mastery checks.
schema.source_question_count: Number of questions in the original bank for this role/topic.

roles.role_mission: adapt advanced ML methods to product problems through experiments, ablations, causal thinking, and rigorous empirical evidence
roles.quality_bar: claims are backed by controlled comparisons, uncertainty estimates, and product-relevant tradeoff analysis
reading_strategy: Read the first pass for vocabulary and assumptions.
Read the second pass by building a small artifact for each topic.
For every topic, write one failure mode, one diagnostic, one stakeholder caveat, and one production or governance implication.
Treat medium questions as application checks and hard questions as failure-mode, tradeoff, and design-reasoning checks.

topics.learning_objective: Master multi-armed bandits well enough to apply it in the Applied ML Scientist role: define the assumptions, choose the right method or design, detect subtle failure modes, and explain tradeoffs to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
topics.overview: This module treats multi-armed bandits as a medium-to-hard job skill for a Applied ML Scientist. Read it through the lens of empirical research, domain adaptation, statistical evidence, and practical model impact. The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as research prototype, ablation study, offline-online validation.
topics.role_application: For a Applied ML Scientist, multi-armed bandits matters because the role's mission is to adapt advanced ML methods to product problems through experiments, ablations, causal thinking, and rigorous empirical evidence. The expected quality bar is that claims are backed by controlled comparisons, uncertainty estimates, and product-relevant tradeoff analysis. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect multi-armed bandits to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for multi-armed bandits: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for multi-armed bandits to be valid in a realistic Applied ML Scientist workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Study ranking as a multi-stage decision system: retrieval, filtering, ranking, reranking, business rules, and online feedback. Define the user value and guardrails before optimizing CTR or relevance. While studying multi-armed bandits, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Learn two-tower retrieval, approximate nearest neighbors, negative sampling, learning-to-rank losses, calibration, reranking, and online serving. Understand how candidate recall constrains all downstream rankers. While studying multi-armed bandits, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Compare offline metrics with online experiments, counterfactual estimates, and guardrails. Watch for position bias, popularity bias, feedback loops, novelty loss, and interference between users or items. While studying multi-armed bandits, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: System tradeoffs
reading_sections.reading_note: Ranking quality competes with latency, freshness, diversity, monetization, fairness, and catalog constraints. Senior work is often about balancing these objectives explicitly. While studying multi-armed bandits, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

practice_lab.title: Applied lab: multi-armed bandits for Applied ML Scientist
practice_lab.setup: Create a realistic mini-scenario where a Applied ML Scientist must make or defend a decision involving multi-armed bandits.
tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about multi-armed bandits.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for multi-armed bandits.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply multi-armed bandits: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: design a multistage ranking pipeline and identify metrics at each stage
compute NDCG for a manually ranked list and interpret position weights
write an A/B plan with relevance, latency, diversity, and fairness guardrails
common_pitfalls: optimizing CTR while harming long-term satisfaction
sampling negatives that make offline metrics look better than online impact
ignoring candidate-generation recall when debugging ranker quality
using logged data without correcting for exposure bias
mastery_check: Explain multi-armed bandits without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for multi-armed bandits and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for multi-armed bandits.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of multi-armed bandits, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for multi-armed bandits, and what companion evidence would you require?

The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as research paper, benchmark, training objective.
topics.role_application: For a AI Research Scientist, scaling laws matters because the role's mission is to create and validate new AI methods, theories, evaluations, and experimental findings that advance model capabilities or safety. The expected quality bar is that novel claims survive ablations, statistical scrutiny, reproducibility checks, and alternative explanations. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect scaling laws to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for scaling laws: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for scaling laws to be valid in a realistic AI Research Scientist workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Start with the claim: what is new, what baseline it improves over, and what mechanism is hypothesized. Research reading should separate empirical results, theoretical assumptions, and author interpretation. While studying scaling laws, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Study experimental controls, data construction, optimization setup, scaling behavior, ablations, hyperparameter fairness, and statistical testing. For theory-heavy topics, track assumptions and what is actually proven. While studying scaling laws, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Ask whether the benchmark measures the intended capability, whether contamination or cherry-picking is possible, and whether results survive seeds, data slices, model sizes, and alternative baselines. While studying scaling laws, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Communication
reading_sections.reading_note: Practice writing concise research notes: hypothesis, setup, controls, result, uncertainty, limitation, and next experiment. Good scientists make uncertainty legible. While studying scaling laws, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

practice_lab.title: Applied lab: scaling laws for AI Research Scientist
practice_lab.setup: Create a realistic mini-scenario where a AI Research Scientist must make or defend a decision involving scaling laws.
tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about scaling laws.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for scaling laws.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply scaling laws: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: reproduce a small ablation table from scratch
write a one-page critique of benchmark validity
design the next experiment that would most reduce uncertainty
common_pitfalls: claiming novelty without strong baselines
confusing correlation in scaling plots with causal mechanism
ignoring negative results and failed ablations
overgeneralizing from one dataset or one seed
mastery_check: Explain scaling laws without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for scaling laws and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for scaling laws.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of scaling laws, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for scaling laws, and what companion evidence would you require?

Define the unit of prediction: token, span, sentence, document, conversation turn, or retrieval result. While studying subword tokenization, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Learn tokenization, embeddings, transformer masks, fine-tuning, sequence labeling, extraction, retrieval, reranking, summarization, and multilingual transfer. Tie each technique to the structure of the text task. While studying subword tokenization, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Use metrics that match the task granularity. Inspect boundary errors, negation, temporal references, entity ambiguity, domain drift, label noise, and calibration rather than relying only on aggregate scores. While studying subword tokenization, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Deployment concerns
reading_sections.reading_note: Text logs often contain sensitive data. Design privacy controls, redaction, access rules, and monitoring for semantic drift or harmful outputs. While studying subword tokenization, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

practice_lab.title: Applied lab: subword tokenization for NLP Engineer
practice_lab.setup: Create a realistic mini-scenario where a NLP Engineer must make or defend a decision involving subword tokenization.
tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about subword tokenization.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for subword tokenization.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply subword tokenization: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: create an annotation guide with hard examples
build an error taxonomy by linguistic phenomenon
compare dense retrieval and cross-encoder reranking on ambiguous queries
common_pitfalls: using document-level metrics for token-level failures
ignoring annotation guideline ambiguity
assuming multilingual transfer works equally across language families
trusting lexical overlap metrics for semantic correctness
mastery_check: Explain subword tokenization without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for subword tokenization and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for subword tokenization.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of subword tokenization, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for subword tokenization, and what companion evidence would you require?
